title: Average Salary Australia: How to Convert Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay
description: Learn how to convert your hourly rate to annual salary using the 38-hour week. Includes National Minimum Wage, award rates, casual loading, super, and tax for 2026–27.
salarySummary: For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week, annual gross pay is hourly rate × 38 × 52, with super paid on top.

faqs.q: How do I convert my hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work per week, then by 52 weeks. For a standard full-time role, assume 38 hours per week. For example, $30/hour × 38 × 52 = $59,280 gross per year. This calculation does not include overtime, penalty rates, or allowances.

faqs.q: Does casual loading affect my annual salary calculation?
faqs.a: Yes. Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate. If your base rate is $26.44 (National Minimum Wage), the casual rate is $33.05. When calculating annual pay, use the casual rate if you are a casual employee. The loading is part of your ordinary earnings for superannuation purposes.

faqs.q: How is superannuation calculated on my annual salary?
faqs.a: Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at 12% (from 1 July 2026). For a full-time employee earning $60,000 gross, the employer contributes an additional $7,200 per year, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. Super is not deducted from your pay; it is an extra benefit.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Annual Salary Calculation

When you receive an hourly rate or a salary offer, the first step is to convert it to an annual figure. The standard formula used across Australia is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**

This assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. For most full-time roles, the benchmark is 38 hours per week, as defined by the Fair Work Ombudsman. If your offer is based on a different weekly hours, adjust accordingly.

### The 38-Hour Week Assumption

In Australia, the standard full-time working week is 38 hours. When you see an annual salary figure, it is almost always based on this assumption. For example, if your hourly rate is $35, your annual gross pay would be:

$35 × 38 × 52 = $69,160 per year

This is the gross amount before tax and Medicare. It also does not include superannuation, which is paid on top by your employer.

### National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

The **National Minimum Wage** from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. This is the legal minimum for employees not covered by an award or registered agreement. However, most industries have **award rates** that are higher. Award rates are set by the Fair Work Commission and vary by industry and occupation. They often include higher rates for overtime, weekends, and public holidays.

If you are comparing a salary offer, check whether it meets the relevant award minimum. The **average salary australia** figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) are useful benchmarks, but they are averages across all industries and states, not a median for your specific job.

### Casual Loading and Superannuation

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for lack of paid leave. For the National Minimum Wage, the casual rate is $33.05 per hour ($26.44 × 1.25). When calculating annual pay for a casual role, use the loaded rate. For example, a casual earning $33.05 per hour working 38 hours per week would have an annual gross of:

$33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,306.80

**Superannuation** is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at 12% (from 1 July 2026). The employer contributes this amount to your super fund. It is not deducted from your pay. The maximum contribution base is $270,830 per year, meaning super is capped at $32,499.60 per year.

### Tax and Medicare

For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:

- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15% of excess over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: $4,020 plus 30% of excess over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: $31,020 plus 37% of excess over $135,000
- $190,001+: $51,420 plus 45% of excess over $190,000

Medicare levy is generally 2% of taxable income. The reduction thresholds for singles and families are based on 2025–26 figures as 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed in this estimate. This estimate does not include the Medicare levy surcharge, HELP repayments, or salary packaging.

### Using the Average Salary Australia Data

The ABS publishes **Average Weekly Earnings (AWE)** twice a year. For May 2026, the full-time adult ordinary time earnings were $2,083.70 per week, which equates to an annual salary of approximately $108,352.40 ($2,083.70 × 52). All employees total earnings (including part-time) were $1,579.20 per week, or about $82,118.40 per year.

These are **averages**, not medians for your specific job. They include all industries and states. If you are researching the **average salary australia** for your role, use these figures as a broad reference, but consult industry-specific data from the Fair Work Ombudsman or your award.

### Fortnightly Pay and Budgeting

Many Australian employees are paid fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross pay, multiply your weekly pay by 2. For a full-time worker on the National Minimum Wage:

$1,004.90 per week × 2 = $2,009.80 per fortnight

This is useful for budgeting and comparing with salary offers that are quoted fortnightly.

### Important Disclaimer

Annual pay calculated here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.

For more details, see the [the timesheet](/) to calculate your own figures, or refer to [pay guides](/blog) for award-specific information. You can also explore [reference tables](/data) for tax and super rates, or read about [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) and [take-home pay](/topics/take-home).
